title: A linear recurrence bounds the shift span
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field], $m\geq0$, $d\geq1$ integers, $a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1}\in K$, and $(c_n)_{n\geq0}$ a sequence in $K$ satisfying the linear recurrence of order $d$ with coefficients $a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1}$ from the index $m$ on [def-weil-eventual-linear-recurrence]. For $j\geq0$ let $R_j=(c_{j+s})_{s\geq0}\in K^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$. Then every $R_j$ lies in the $K$-linear span [def-weil-submodule-span] of $R_0,\ldots,R_{m+d-1}$. Consequently the subspace $V\subseteq K^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$ [def-weil-sequence-subspace] spanned by all $R_j$ is finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] with $\dim_KV\leq m+d$ [def-weil-vector-space-dimension].

source.place: ## Proof, third paragraph ('(3) also directly implies (2): ... All rows therefore lie in the span of $R_0,\ldots,R_{m+d-1}$'); stated without proof in literature/milne-lectures-on-etale-cohomology_LEC.pdf, p. 157, Bourbaki's Exercise 3(d)

proof.text: For $j\geq m$ and $s\geq0$, apply the assumed recurrence [def-weil-eventual-linear-recurrence] at $n=j+s$, which satisfies $n\geq m$. It gives $c_{j+s+d}=-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}a_i c_{j+s+i}$. Since sequence addition and scalar multiplication are coordinatewise [def-weil-sequence-subspace], equality in every coordinate $s$ gives the sequence identity $R_{j+d}=-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}a_iR_{j+i}$. Thus this identity holds for every $j\geq m$.

source.place: third paragraph, final sentences, lines 27-30: '(3) also directly implies (2)' and 'All rows therefore lie in the span of R_0,...,R_{m+d-1}'; apply the scalar recurrence in each coordinate

proof.text: Using the span definition [def-weil-submodule-span], put $W=\operatorname{span}_K\{R_0,\ldots,R_{m+d-1}\}$. Prove $R_k\in W$ for all $k\geq0$ by strong induction on $k$. If $k<m+d$, this is one of the defining generators. If $k\geq m+d$, set $j=k-d\geq m$; the identity of step 1 gives $R_k=-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}a_iR_{k-d+i}$. For every $0\leq i<d$, $0\leq k-d+i<k$, so the induction hypothesis puts each summand vector in $W$. The closure under scalar multiplication and addition in [def-weil-sequence-subspace], including multiplication by $-1$, puts $R_k$ in $W$. This establishes the first conclusion without assuming any of the initial rows independent.

source.place: third paragraph, final sentences, lines 27-30: '(3) also directly implies (2)' and 'All rows therefore lie in the span of R_0,...,R_{m+d-1}'; write out the strong induction hidden in the last sentence

proof.text: Let $W=\operatorname{span}_K\{R_0,\ldots,R_{m+d-1}\}$ as in step 2. By [def-weil-submodule-span], a span is the smallest subspace containing its generators. Step 2 shows that $W$ contains every $R_k$, so $V\subseteq W$. Conversely $V$ contains each generator of $W$, so $W\subseteq V$. Hence $V=W$. To see directly that every element of $V$ is a finite linear combination of the initial rows, the set $U=\{\sum_{i=0}^{m+d-1}\lambda_iR_i:\lambda_i\in K\}$ is a subspace: zero uses all zero coefficients, the sum of two such vectors adds their coefficients, and scalar multiplication multiplies their coefficients [def-weil-sequence-subspace]. It contains every initial row, so $W\subseteq U$ by the smallest-subspace characterization; the reverse inclusion follows from closure of $W$ under finite sums and scalar multiplication. Thus the $m+d$ initial rows span $V$ in the sense of [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], proving finite-dimensionality.

source.place: third paragraph, final sentences, lines 27-30: '(3) also directly implies (2)' and 'All rows therefore lie in the span of R_0,...,R_{m+d-1}'; identify the full shift span with the initial finite span

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-span-independent-subfamily] to the finite family $R_0,\ldots,R_{m+d-1}$. It supplies a subset $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,m+d-1\}$ such that $(R_i)_{i\in S}$ is independent and has the same span as all the initial rows, namely $V$ by step 3 (the cited statement uses indices $1,\ldots,m+d$, which are relabelled by subtracting $1$). Write $k=|S|$ and list its elements in increasing order. Apply [lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family] to this independent list of $k$ vectors: its span is $V$, so $\dim_KV=k$. Since $S$ is a subset of an index set with $m+d$ elements, $k\leq m+d$. Therefore $\dim_KV\leq m+d$. This requires no independence, distinctness or nonvanishing of the original family.

lean.statement: theorem shift_span_bound {K : Type u} [Field K] (m d : ℕ) (hd : 1 ≤ d) (a : Fin d → K) (c : ℕ → K) (hrec : (⟨d, fun i ↦ -a i⟩ : LinearRecurrence K).IsSolution (fun n ↦ c (n + m))) : (∀ j : ℕ, (fun s : ℕ ↦ c (j + s)) ∈ Submodule.span K (Set.range (fun i : Fin (m + d) ↦ fun s : ℕ ↦ c (i.val + s)))) ∧ FiniteDimensional K (Submodule.span K (Set.range (fun j : ℕ ↦ fun s : ℕ ↦ c (j + s)))) ∧ Module.finrank K (Submodule.span K (Set.range (fun j : ℕ ↦ fun s : ℕ ↦ c (j + s)))) ≤ m + d
